t: #2556 — Disconnect Path in a Binary Matrix by at Most One Flip
o: Movement is only right or down through 1-cells. We may flip at most one cell (not the corners) and want to make (0,0) unreachable from (m−1,n−1). If no path exists already, the answer is trivially true. Otherwise, by Menger's theorem the answer is false exactly when two vertex-disjoint paths exist; equivalently, it is true exactly when some single cell lies on every path. Practical plan: find one path, then test whether deleting each internal cell of that path breaks connectivity — if the minimum vertex cut is 1, its cut vertex must lie on our chosen path.
k: If no path exists, return true immediately (flip nothing).
If the s–t minimum vertex cut is 1, the cut vertex appears on every path, hence on any single path we find.
Testing each internal cell of one found path with a fresh BFS is correct: if no single deletion disconnects, two disjoint paths exist and the answer is false.

a.n: Approach 1: Find a path, then test deletions
a.i: Run a BFS with parent pointers to obtain one monotone path. If none exists return true. Otherwise, for each internal cell of the path, temporarily treat it as blocked and re-run BFS; if any deletion disconnects the corners, return true. If none does, two disjoint paths exist (any cut vertex would have been on our path), so return false.
s: BFS from (0,0) moving right/down over 1-cells, recording parents.
If (m−1,n−1) is unreached, return true; otherwise reconstruct the path.
For each internal path cell, re-run BFS with that cell blocked.
Return true if any BFS fails, else false.
a.t: O((m+n)·m·n) worst case — one BFS per internal path cell (at most m+n−2 of them); fast in practice since disconnection is usually detected early.

w: An interview-safe alternative framing: the answer is false iff two vertex-disjoint monotone paths exist (Menger). The delete-and-retest method exploits that any unique cut vertex must lie on the specific path we found. Edge cases: 1×1 grid (already 'disconnected'? corners can't be flipped — here start equals end, treat carefully), grids with no path at all, and single-row/single-column grids (always true unless already blocked). A follow-up is to solve it in strictly O(m·n) using articulation-point ideas on the DAG.
